This internal RND primitive adapts the forward loop from original Soup
[`d500ae0d`](https://github.com/MakazhanAlpamys/Soup/tree/d500ae0dca7c4da905f8d59c9866af2f8aaa824b).
It reuses the [B1.1 cache codec](expert-shard-format.md), preserves the native
eager arithmetic and loads one routed expert at a time. Experts without tokens
are not read. Coverage can approach 100%, so reduced disk reads are not promised.

B1.3 adds first-order backward through frozen routed experts and internal
DeepSeek-V3 runtime/L2L integration. Non-expert LoRA adapters can train; routed
base weights and adapters on routed experts remain unsupported. Backward refetches
each frozen expert inside a bounded lease and accepts only the validated stateless
SiLU activation without hooks; higher-order gradients are refused. The routing weight
multiplies the per-expert node's output with ordinary autograd, so its gradient needs no
reload.
The public L2L launch guard admits Llama/Mistral, and DeepSeek-V3 only with
`stream_expert_layout: per_expert`; planner, budgets and defaults are unchanged. The only
public expert-training entry point is the opt-in B6 recipe below.

CPU and CUDA tiny-model tests compare gradients with resident controls and
exercise optimizer updates and adapter reload. The opt-in SFT configuration is
`training.stream_expert_layout: per_expert`, with `stream_source: disk`. Its disk
preflight currently requires a new single-disk NF4 cache without double quant.
The default remains fused storage. Real giant results and limitations belong in
[the B6 record](../benchmarks/b6-giant-moe-20261028.md).

Meta construction keeps native fused expert factories on the meta device,
avoiding a temporary giant CPU reservation before parameter registration.
Normal model buffers keep their constructor values; a changed expert
constructor that introduces buffers is refused instead of losing those values.

`plan_expert_buffer(reader, dtype=...)` computes a single weight slot independent
of expert count. `ExpertBufferPool` allocates one byte arena with aligned views
for dense gate/up and down matrices, packed weights, statistics, shared NF4 code
tables and explicit nested-statistics scratch. The budget includes padding.
An insufficient budget fails before allocating the arena or reading an expert.
On CUDA, the runtime and preflight use `expert_allocation_budget`: logical
storage plus an explicit 32 MiB allocator reserve. Observed allocator growth is
checked against that finite budget before the first expert read. Different
allocator configurations can still exceed the reserve and fail explicitly.

CUDA NF4 decoding uses bitsandbytes `out` kernels directly into this arena.
Missing CUDA kernels fail explicitly; there is no allocating CUDA fallback.
CPU bitsandbytes 0.50.2 has no such `out` kernels, so CPU development checks use
temporary CPU dequantization results before copying into the arena. The CPU
arena bound does not bound those CPU temporaries or the entire process RSS.

Activations, routing masks, GEMM/backend workspaces, context memory and allocator
reservations are separate from the expert-weight budget. Record total CUDA peak
allocated **and** reserved memory separately; do not describe a 64 MiB weight
arena as a 64 MiB total-VRAM requirement. Host staging also has its own byte count.

One aligned CPU staging buffer is reused. Returned expert weights never alias
staging, but they alias the reusable compute arena and are valid only inside
`pool.lease(reader, expert)`. Nested/concurrent leases and closing an active lease
are refused. Copies are blocking; CUDA synchronizes before releasing a lease,
including on errors. This intentionally favors explicit lifetime safety, with
no asynchronous-prefetch or throughput claim.

Readers sharing a pool must agree on shapes, NF4 specs and stored dtype, and fit
its staging span. The pool owns its buffers; the caller owns and closes readers.
`pool.close()` releases buffer references, not PyTorch's global caching allocator.

`streamed_experts_class()` is lazy, so importing the module does not import
torch, transformers, bitsandbytes or PEFT. Its module accepts hidden states
`[tokens, H]`, int64 expert indices `[tokens, k]` and finite routing weights of the
same shape/device. The hidden dtype must match the pool. Expert IDs are visited
in ascending order; token gather, gate/up activation, down projection, route
weighting and index-add follow the resident eager implementation.

The B1.1 codec is the storage layer, not a public training option or a speed,
quality or whole-model VRAM claim. B1.2/B1.3 now provide the internal sequential
expert [forward/backward and runtime/L2L path](expert-forward.md); public
expert-streamed enablement and planner/YAML/CLI changes remain B1.4.

The codec is adapted from original Soup's `utils/expert_stream.py` at
[`d500ae0d`](https://github.com/MakazhanAlpamys/Soup/tree/d500ae0dca7c4da905f8d59c9866af2f8aaa824b).
Only the writer, reader and storage validation are reused. RND's B2 skeleton
layout, Kimi K2 aliases, FP8 source decoder and adapter preflight remain in place.

`shard_checkpoint(..., expert_layout="per_expert")` is an internal storage API.
It currently admits the canonical `deepseek_v3` architecture with a B2
`ShardLayout(stack_experts=True)`, and source checkpoints with separate
`mlp.experts.<id>.{gate,up,down}_proj.weight` matrices. Expert ids must start at
zero, be contiguous and agree across projections. Fused-only source tensors and
other architectures are refused. Existing/default calls keep the fused format.

The writer collects one layer's stored expert tensors in host memory before
writing its file. The expert execution arena does not bound this preparation
peak. Peak RAM for preparing a real DeepSeek-V3 or Kimi K2 checkpoint has not
been measured; a 32 GB host is not established to fit.

The header-only cache budget defaults to FP32 upper bounds for non-expert
weights. An explicit decoder layer count and exact NF4 suffix selection can
tighten that bound to the actual writer layout, while retaining the largest
layer, vocab-copy and metadata reserves. The B6 source planner reads bounded
ranges from a pinned checkpoint, then verifies every planned header/size and
the model config against the full downloaded files. Its harness independently
matches the plan to the constructed writer layout before conversion. All source
payloads are still downloaded; per-write free-space checks remain in force.

Each routed expert E has `E.gate_up` with shape `[2I, H]` (gate rows then up
rows) and `E.down` with shape `[H, I]`. The integer expert id and these names map
back to the original gate/up/down names; the cache does not retain the original
three-key representation. All MoE layers must agree on expert count and shapes.
FP8 sources use B3's block-scale decoder before conversion/packing.

Under NF4 each expert matrix is quantized independently, storing the existing
packed tensor, `::absmax`, and, when enabled, `::nested_absmax` and
`::nested_offset`. Logical shapes, dtype, block sizes and nested flag are in
`expert_quant_specs`. Shared NF4 code tables are checked for consistency across
matrices and saved in extras. RND's FP8-source double-quant policy is unchanged.

Missing expert fields mean the unchanged fused format. Unsupported versions,
inconsistent dimensions/counts and malformed NF4 metadata fail explicitly.
Changing layouts or losing a referenced expert file causes a cache miss.
B2's `stacked_experts`, `fp32_keys`, layer-count and source-identity checks remain
part of the cache key. Expert files follow their layer's stripe-root placement.
Switching back to fused can leave unused expert files; no active index references
them. This change does not delete unrelated files or old stripe roots.

Before converting fused storage to per-expert storage or back, the sharder
invalidates the previous index before rewriting any cache file, including under
`force=True`. If a write or final index commit fails, no reusable index describes
the partial conversion; requesting either layout rebuilds it. Partial files are
retained for that rebuild, not rolled back. If index invalidation itself fails,
conversion stops before any shard write. Same-layout stripe relocation retains
its existing index commit and deferred stale-file deletion behavior.

The model builder validates the architecture and Hub-code policy through its
meta-only skeleton before reading any index field (the B2 refusal order).
B1.3 then accepts this layout internally: it installs expert readers and one
bounded shared arena before mapping layer weights, and the runtime owns their
lifecycle. Routed base weights stay frozen and expert adapters remain refused;
non-expert LoRA is supported. Existing/default sharder calls still use fused
storage, no public YAML/CLI field is added, and the public L2L launch guard stays
Llama/Mistral. Older RND releases do not understand this extension: use a separate
cache directory and re-shard as fused before downgrading.

[B1.2/B1.3 streamed experts](expert-forward.md) provide an internal sequential
forward primitive, first-order backward through frozen routed experts, and internal
runtime/L2L integration for native DeepSeek-V3. The opt-in
`training.stream_expert_layout: per_expert` supports experimental frozen-expert
SFT with attention/shared-expert adapters. The narrow disk preflight requires
a new cache, one disk, NF4 without double quant and readable source headers.
Routed experts stay frozen, with no expert adapters. One bounded expert arena is
not a bound on total allocated/reserved VRAM. Tiny-model CPU and CUDA checks cover
backward and adapter reload; no real giant checkpoint has yet been validated.
See `benchmarks/b6-giant-moe-20261028.md`. Public MoE L2L launch, planner and
defaults remain unchanged (B1.4).

`soup infer` and `soup bench infer` accept `--cuda-graphs`. On a resident Qwen2 or Llama model,
optionally with one LoRA adapter from `soup train`, generation replays CUDA graphs instead of
launching every kernel from Python. The default path is unchanged.

Measured on an RTX 5070 Laptop (Windows, unpinned, fresh processes, A-B-B-A-B-A) with
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in FP16, 128 greedy tokens per request: the slowest run with the flag was
**2.9x** the fastest run without it (60.1 vs 20.7 tok/s), and **2.8x** under an unmerged LoRA
(49.2 vs 17.8 tok/s), with identical token IDs on every request and +42 MiB of reserved VRAM.
`soup infer` over 24 prompts of varied length, model load and compile included, took 96-102 s with
the flag against 131-282 s without. Without the flag the run-to-run spread is large (13.5-20.7 tok/s):
the decode is bound by the host launching ~1,200 kernels per token, and Windows moves that thread
between the hybrid CPU's fast and slow cores; with the flag the spread is 4%. The record is
[`benchmarks/gate-v0.76.0-cuda-graph-decode.md`](../benchmarks/gate-v0.76.0-cuda-graph-decode.md).

- **Cold start is slower.** Before the first row, Soup runs one greedy warm-up on your longest
  prompt, which compiles and captures the graph (about 8-10 s on that card) and sizes the static
  cache once for the whole batch. A one-prompt run can take longer overall. The summary panel's
  `Duration` and `Throughput` start after the warm-up.
- **Outputs are the same.** The flag changes no precision, sampling or stopping rule; sampled rows
  use the temperature you asked for, and the warm-up is greedy so it consumes no sampling RNG. A
  LoRA adapter stays unmerged, exactly as without the flag.
- **Supported:** stock Qwen2/Llama classes, one CUDA GPU, unquantized weights, and at most one
  active plain LoRA adapter. Anything else (quantization, CPU/disk offload, layer streaming, DoRA
  or other LoRA variants, several adapters, flash attention, ASR) is refused before any output is
  written, and every refusal ends with `Omit --cuda-graphs`.
- **Needs PyTorch >= 2.14.** It uses private PyTorch compiler APIs validated on 2.14.0 (it fixes an
  accounting defect in the stock `cudagraphs` backend that otherwise clones every weight into the
  graph pool). Older versions, or a changed API, are refused with a one-line message.
- **Not in `soup chat` or `soup serve`.** A chat history grows every turn, and a static cache that
  grows recompiles every turn.
- **Unmeasured:** `--max-tokens` far above 128 (each K/V update costs an extra copy per step, growing
  with prompt + max_tokens), Linux/macOS, batch sizes above 1, and architectures other than Qwen2.
  Over a 1024-prompt batch the graph tree re-records about once per three rows without any eager
  fallback or memory growth.

`--device` decides where these commands load the model. Without it, the
device is auto-detected and the same rules apply to what was detected (this
also covers `soup bench`, which loads through the `soup infer` path).

`soup data best-of-n` appends and synchronizes one checkpoint record after each
fully sampled and judged prompt. The default journal is
`<output>.checkpoint.jsonl`; override it with `--checkpoint`. If a sampler or
judge backend fails, Soup reports the completed prompt count and journal path.
Rerun the same command with `--resume` to reuse that exact prefix without
sampling it again. The prompt sequence and generation options are bound into the
journal, so changing them makes resume fail closed.

Final SFT and optional DPO JSONL files are published only after every prompt is
complete. The manifest (default `<output>.manifest.json`, or `--manifest`) is
written last and records their row counts and SHA-256 digests. Consumers should
treat only files listed by that final manifest as committed output. Invalid
local data such as a non-finite judge score remains a validation failure rather
than being presented as a recoverable backend outage.

For offline Best-of-N, the candidate and judgment artifacts are the recovery
checkpoint. Offline materialization rejects `--resume` and `--checkpoint`; rerun
the exact materialization command after a late failure. The final manifest is
written last and is the only commit marker; consumers must verify it and use only
the SFT/DPO files it lists.

`soup mcp serve` runs a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
server over **stdio** (default) or a local **SSE / HTTP** listener, so any MCP client  Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Continue 
can drive Soup conversationally. Install the extra first:

Both bind `127.0.0.1:8765` by default and **require a Bearer token on every
request**. With `--auth-token` omitted, a fresh one is generated at startup and
printed to stderr; it is 16-128 urlsafe-base64 characters, the same shape
`soup ui` uses. Point a client at it with a header:

**Security:**
- **The token is required and there is no opt-out.** A loopback listener is
  reachable by every process on the machine, not just by you.
- **The token travels in the header, never the URL.** There is deliberately no
  query-string fallback, so it cannot be captured in proxy or access logs.
- **DNS-rebinding protection is on.** A request whose `Host` is not the address
  the server bound to is refused with `421`, a foreign `Origin` with `403`.
  This is the gate the Bearer token cannot be: a web page the operator merely
  visits attaches no `Authorization` header, but its request still arrives at
  the port.
- **A non-loopback `--host` prints a warning**, and a wildcard bind (`0.0.0.0`)
  prints a second one  with no single advertised name there is nothing to pin,
  so the Host check degrades to accepting any `Host`.
- **`--host` / `--port` / `--auth-token` are refused under `--transport stdio`**
  rather than silently ignored: stdio has no listener and nothing to authorize.

The server exposes 14 read-only tools  `advise`, `data_inspect`,
`data_validate`, `data_score`, `data_doctor`, `recipes_search`, `recipes_show`,
`runs_list`, `runs_show`, `registry_list`, `registry_show`, `profile`,
`diagnose_evidence`, `ship_evidence`  each returning JSON. Two **plan-only**
mutating tools (`train_start`, `export`) are gated behind `--allow-mutating`
(`"args": ["mcp", "serve", "--allow-mutating"]`); when `--allow-mutating` alone is active, they only render the exact command that would run  they never execute training or export.

`--allow-execute` implies `--allow-mutating` and enables full background subprocess execution via two execution tools (`train_execute` and `export_execute`). Execution requires a server-issued one-time confirmation token returned during the planning phase (`train_start` or `export`). The token state is kept in-memory with a 5-minute TTL and is consumed before subprocess invocation.

**Execution Security & Boundaries:**
- **Flag Safety:** `--allow-execute` is default-off and dangerous. `--allow-mutating` alone can NEVER trigger subprocess execution.
- **One-Time Confirmation Tokens:** Authorization requires a server-issued random token. Client confirmation is UX-only; security relies entirely on the server-side token state.
- **Subprocess Isolation:** Execution runs the Soup CLI as an isolated subprocess (`shell=False`, `stdin=DEVNULL`, `cwd` pinned to server startup directory). Child stdout/stderr is redirected to `.soup/mcp-runs/<run_id>.log` to avoid corrupting the MCP JSON-RPC stdio stream. Planning (`train_start` config snapshot) and execution are refused if `.soup` or `.soup/mcp-runs` is a symbolic link or junction, or if a hard link exists at the run log path. Planning also refuses a link or anything already present at the run directory `.soup/mcp-runs/<run_id>`: the snapshot is written only into a run directory the plan has just created, with `config.yaml` created exclusively and without following a link.
- **Concurrency & Disconnects:** Enforces 1 active execution at a time, gated on a persisted run whose process is still alive  so a **restarted** server does not launch a second training while a child from a previous server is still running, and a stale record whose process is gone never blocks execution. A `launching` record (committed before the child process exists, pid not yet written) blocks restart capacity too: it is indistinguishable from "about to spawn", so treating it as live is the safe direction after a crash in that window. If a server crash leaves that row behind, `soup mcp runs reconcile --expunge-launching` removes rows older than five minutes and prints every removed `run_id`; use `--older-than-seconds N` to choose another positive threshold. The command refuses the whole operation if any candidate records a PID that is still alive. Launches run in background (fire-and-forget). Disconnecting the MCP client does not terminate an already-running subprocess.
- **Config Snapshotting & Input Revalidation:** At plan time (`train_start`), the validated config is snapshotted to `.soup/mcp-runs/<run_id>/config.yaml`, and execution uses this snapshot rather than the original mutable config path. External protected inputs (such as datasets and model/checkpoint directories or files) are not frozen in the snapshot; instead, their content digests (computed via SHA-256 for regular files, or deterministic recursive content hashing over sorted relative file paths for directory trees, bounded by file-count and total-byte safety limits) are recorded at plan time and revalidated immediately before spawn. Modifying an external protected input between plan and execute invalidates the token. Modifying the original config path after planning has no effect because execution strictly uses the snapshotted config. Snapshotting freezes only the configuration itself, not external filesystem assets.
- **Every Local Input Is Pinned:** A train plan pins every local file or directory the run reads (model, datasets, reward/teacher/PRM models, reward `.py` files, unlearning sets); an input outside the working directory is refused at plan time, and an input that did not exist at plan time must still not exist at execution.
